t: Wynt a gerdassant trannoeth parth a Dyuet, a Llys Arberth a gyrchyssant, a gwled darparedic oed yno udunt.
l: They it-was-that travelled the-next-day towards Dyfed, and the Court of-Arberth they made-for, and a-feast prepared was there for-them.
i: The next day they travelled towards Dyfed and made for the court at Arberth, and a feast had been prepared for them there.
n: The part opens as Pwyll brings Rhiannon home. Wynt a gerdassant 'they travelled' is the abnormal sentence, the tale's ordinary narrative order: subject, then the particle a, then the verb; it stresses nothing. gerdassant ← kerdassant, third-person plural preterite of kerdet 'walk, travel', softened after a; gyrchyssant ← kyrchyssant, likewise of kyrchu 'make for'. trannoeth 'the next day'. parth a 'towards'. udunt 'for them' is y 'to' conjugated, third person plural. darparedic 'prepared'. Spelling: u = v (Dyuet = Dyfed), -t = -d (gwled = gwledd).

t: Dygyuor y wlat a'r kyuoeth a doeth attunt o'r gwyr goreu a'r gwraged goreu.
l: The-muster of the land and the realm it-was-that came to-them, of the best men and the best women.
i: The whole land and realm gathered to them, the best of its men and the best of its women.
n: Dygyuor 'muster, gathering' (dygyfor) is the subject, put first: the abnormal sentence again, with a doeth 'came', the third-person singular preterite of dyuot 'come'. y wlat 'the land' ← gwlat, softened after the article because it is feminine. kyuoeth 'realm', as always. attunt 'to them' is at conjugated, third person plural. o'r gwyr goreu 'of the best men'; goreu 'best' (gorau) follows its noun. Spelling: k = c (kyuoeth = cyfoeth).

t: Na gwr na gwreic o hynny nyt edewis Riannon, heb rodi rod enwauc idaw, ae o gae, ae o uodrwy, ae o uaen guerthuawr.
l: Neither man nor woman of those did-not-leave Rhiannon without giving a-gift notable to-him, either of a-brooch, or of a-ring, or of a-stone precious.
i: Not a man or woman of them did Rhiannon let go without giving each a notable gift, a brooch or a ring or a precious stone.
n: The object comes first: Na gwr na gwreic o hynny 'neither man nor woman of those', then nyt edewis Riannon 'Rhiannon did not leave'. edewis is the third-person singular preterite (-is) of adaw 'leave' (modern gadael). rodi rod 'giving a gift': rod is rhodd, with r for rh as often. enwauc = enwawc (enwog) 'famous, notable'. idaw 'to him' is masculine for 'each one'. ae … ae 'either … or'. o gae ← cae 'brooch, clasp'; o uodrwy ← modrwy 'ring'; o uaen ← maen 'stone': each softened after o 'of'. guerthuawr 'precious': gu = gw.

t: Gwledychu y wlat a wnaethont yn llwydannus y ulwydyn honno, a'r eil.
l: Ruling the land they-did prosperously that year, and the second.
i: They ruled the land prosperously that year, and the next.
n: Gwledychu … a wnaethont 'ruling … they did' = they ruled: the verbal-noun narrative, a verbal noun first, then a and a form of gwneuthur 'do'. wnaethont is its third-person plural preterite, softened after a. y wlat 'the land' (gwlat, feminine, softened after the article). llwydannus 'prosperous, successful'. y ulwydyn honno 'that year' is an adverb of time; blwydyn is feminine and softened after the article, hence honno. a'r eil 'and the second'.

t: Ac yn dryded ulwydyn, y dechreuis gwyr y wlat dala trymuryt yndunt, o welet gwr kymeint a gerynt a'e harglwyd ac eu brawduaeth, yn dietiued; a'e dyuynnu attunt a wnaethont.
l: And in the-third year, began the men of the land to-hold heaviness-of-mind in-them, from seeing a-man as-much-as they-loved, and their lord and their foster-brother, without-heir; and his summoning to-them they-did.
i: And in the third year the men of the land began to grow heavy-hearted, seeing a man they loved so well, their lord and their foster-brother, without an heir; and they summoned him to them.
n: dryded ulwydyn: tryded 'third' (feminine of trydyd) and blwydyn, both softened as if after the article y; the White Book does not write it (the Red Book has yny dryded) and the sense does not need it, so it is not supplied. y dechreuis 'began': a singular verb before a plural noun subject (gwyr y wlat). dala trymuryt yndunt 'to hold heaviness of mind in them' — trymuryt is trwm 'heavy' + bryt 'mind'; yndunt is yn conjugated, third person plural. gerynt ← kerynt, third-person plural imperfect of caru 'love', softened after the relative a. a'e harglwyd 'and their lord': 'e 'their' puts h before a vowel. brawduaeth 'foster-brother'. dietiued 'heirless' (di- + etiued). a'e dyuynnu 'and summoning him'.

t: Sef lle y doethont y gyt, y Bresseleu yn Dyuet.
l: That-is the place they-came together, to Preseli in Dyfed.
i: The place where they came together was Preseli in Dyfed.
n: Sef 'that is' points at an answer: where did they meet? It is dropped in i. lle y doethont 'the place where they came': doethont is the third-person plural preterite of dyuot. y gyt 'together' (modern ynghyd). y Bresseleu 'to Preseli': Presseleu softened after y 'to'. ss is the scribe's spelling of s.

t: “Arglwyd,” heb wynt, “ni a wdom na bydy gyuoet ti a rei o wyr y wlat honn, ac yn ouyn ni yw, na byd it etiued o'r wreic yssyd gennyt.
l: “Lord,” said they, “we it-is-that know that you-will-not-be contemporary with some of the men of this land, and our fear it-is, that there-will-not-be to-you an-heir of the wife that-is with-you.
i: “Lord,” they said, “we know that you will not outlast some of the men of this land, and our fear is that you will have no heir by the wife you have.
n: ni a wdom 'we know': wdom ← gwdom, first-person plural present of gwybot, the g lost after a. na bydy 'that you will not be': bydy is the second-person singular future of bot. gyuoet ← kyuoet 'contemporary, of the same age', softened as the complement of bydy. The sense seems to be that he will not live as long as some of his men; the phrasing is compressed, and i takes it so. yn ouyn ni yw 'our fear it is': yn here is the old spelling of ein 'our'. na byd it 'that there will not be to you': it is y 'to' conjugated, second person. yssyd 'that is', the relative form of bot. gennyt 'with you'.

t: Ac wrth hynny, kymmer wreic arall y bo ettiued yt ohonei.
l: And for that, take a-wife other that may-be an-heir to-you from-her.
i: And so take another wife, by whom you may have an heir.
n: wrth hynny 'for that, therefore'. kymmer 'take' is the second-person singular imperative of kymryt. wreic ← gwreic, softened as the object of the verb. y bo 'that there may be': bo is the present subjunctive of bot. ettiued 'heir', spelt here with tt (etiued in the unit before). yt 'to you' is another spelling of it. ohonei 'from her' is o conjugated, third person feminine.

t: Nyt byth,” heb wynt, “y perhey di, a chyt kerych di uot yuelly, nys diodefwn y gennyt.”
l: Not for-ever,” said they, “will-you-last you, and though you-may-wish you to-be thus, we-will-not-suffer-it from-you.”
i: You will not last for ever,” they said, “and though you may wish to stay as you are, we will not suffer it from you.”
n: Nyt byth … y perhey di 'not for ever will you last': the adverb is put first and negated with nyt, and the verb follows with y. perhey is the second-person singular present of parhau 'last', with future sense. a chyt 'and though' (kyt, spirant after a). kerych is the second-person singular present subjunctive of caru 'love, wish', the subjunctive after kyt. uot ← bot, softened as the object of kerych. yuelly is uelly (felly) 'thus' with a prefixed y. nys diodefwn 'we will not suffer it': ny + the infixed 's 'it', and diodefwn, first-person plural present of diodef 'endure'. y gennyt 'from you'.

t: “Ie,” heb y Pwyll, “nyt hir ettwa yd ym y gyt, a llawer damwein a digawn bot.
l: “Yes,” said Pwyll, “not long yet are-we together, and many a-chance can be.
i: “Yes,” said Pwyll, “we have not been together long yet, and many things may happen.
n: heb y Pwyll: after heb 'said' a name often takes the article y, as throughout the tale. nyt hir 'not long' is put first. ettwa (modern eto) 'yet'. yd ym 'we are': ym is the first-person plural present of bot, with yd, the form of y before a vowel. llawer damwein 'many a chance' — llawer takes a singular noun. a digawn bot 'that can be': digawn is the third-person singular present of the verb digawn 'be able', here 'can happen'.

t: Oedwch a mi hynn hyt ym pen y ulwydyn; a blwydyn y'r amser hwnn, ni a wnawn yr oet y dyuot y gyt, ac wrth ych kynghor y bydaf.”
l: Delay with me this until the-end of the year; and a-year to this time, we it-is-that will-make the appointment to come together, and by your counsel I-will-be.”
i: Give me this much delay, until the end of the year; and a year from now we will appoint a time to meet, and I will abide by your counsel.”
n: Oedwch 'delay' is the second-person plural imperative of oedi 'put off'; Oedwch a mi hynn 'delay with me this much'. ym pen 'at the end' is yn 'in' + pen: yn becomes ym before p, and the nasal mutation (ym mhen) is not written. y'r amser hwnn 'to this time' = from now. ni a wnawn 'we will make': wnawn is the first-person plural present of gwneuthur, softened after a. oet 'appointment, appointed time'. wrth ych kynghor 'by your counsel'. y bydaf 'I will be', first-person singular future of bot.

t: Yr oet a wnaethant.
l: The appointment they-made.
i: They made the appointment.
n: The object is put first, then a and the verb: Yr oet 'the appointment', a wnaethant 'they made'. wnaethant is another spelling of wnaethont, the third-person plural preterite of gwneuthur.

t: Kynn dyuot cwbyl o'r oet, mab a anet idaw ef, ac yn Arberth y ganet.
l: Before coming the-whole of the appointment, a-son it-was-that was-born to-him, and in Arberth was-he-born.
i: Before the appointed time had fully come, a son was born to him, born at Arberth.
n: Kynn dyuot 'before coming': kynn 'before' with a verbal noun. cwbyl o'r oet 'the whole of the appointed time'. mab a anet 'a son was born': anet ← ganet, the impersonal preterite of geni 'bear', the g lost after a. idaw ef 'to him'. yn Arberth y ganet 'in Arberth he was born' — the phrase is put first and the verb follows with the particle y, which does not soften it.

t: A'r nos y ganet, y ducpwyt gwraged y wylat y mab a'y uam.
l: And the night he-was-born, were-brought women to watch the boy and his mother.
i: And on the night he was born, women were brought in to watch over the boy and his mother.
n: A'r nos 'and the night' is an adverb of time. y ducpwyt 'were brought' is the impersonal preterite of dwyn 'bring, carry'; the impersonal has no person, and gwraged is its object. y wylat 'to watch': gwylat (gwylied), softened after y 'to'. a'y uam 'and his mother': mam softened after 'y 'his'.

t: Sef a wnaeth y gwraged kyscu, a mam y mab, Riannon.
l: That-is what did the women: sleeping, and the mother of the boy, Rhiannon.
i: The women fell asleep, and so did the boy's mother, Rhiannon.
n: Sef a wnaeth y gwraged kyscu 'that is what the women did: sleeping'. Sef points at the answer and is dropped in i. wnaeth is singular although y gwraged is plural: a verb before its noun subject stays singular. kyscu 'sleep' (cysgu); sc is the old spelling of sg.

t: Sef riuedi o wraged a ducpwyt y'r ystauell hwech wraged.
l: That-is the number of women that were-brought to the chamber: six women.
i: Six women had been brought into the chamber.
n: Sef riuedi … hwech wraged 'that is the number … six women'. riuedi (rhifedi) 'number'. o wraged 'of women' — gwraged softened after o. a ducpwyt 'that were brought', the impersonal preterite again. y'r ystauell 'to the chamber' (ystafell). hwech is chwech 'six', spelt with hw (the Red Book has chwech). wraged after the numeral is softened as written in both witnesses; the plural after a numeral is not the ordinary rule.

t: Gwylat a wnaethont wynteu dalym o'r nos, ac yn hynny eisswys, kyn hanner noss, kyscu a wnaeth pawb ohonunt, a thu a'r pylgeint deffroi.
l: Watching they-did, they-for-their-part, a-while of the night, and in that nevertheless, before half night, sleeping did everyone of-them, and towards the dawn-hour waking.
i: They kept watch for part of the night, but even so, before midnight, every one of them fell asleep, and towards dawn they woke.
n: Gwylat a wnaethont wynteu 'watching they did, they for their part'. dalym ← talym 'a while', softened as an adverb of time. ac yn hynny eisswys 'and in that, nevertheless': eisswys is eissoes 'yet, however'. kyn hanner noss 'before midnight'; noss is nos with ss. kyscu a wnaeth pawb 'everyone slept': pawb takes a singular verb. ohonunt 'of them' (o conjugated, third person plural). a thu a'r pylgeint 'and towards the pylgeint': tu 'side' with the spirant after a; pylgeint (plygain) is the early hour before dawn. deffroi 'waking' carries on from a wnaeth without a second verb.

t: A phan deffroyssant, edrych a orugant y lle y dodyssynt y mab, ac nyt oed dim ohonaw yno.
l: And when they-woke, looking they-did at the place where they-had-put the boy, and there-was-not anything of-him there.
i: And when they woke, they looked to the place where they had put the boy, and there was no sign of him there.
n: A phan 'and when': pan with the spirant after a. deffroyssant 'they woke', third-person plural preterite. edrych a orugant 'looking they did': orugant is the third-person plural preterite of the other verb 'do' (goruc), softened after a. y lle 'the place' = to the place. y dodyssynt 'where they had put': dodyssynt is the third-person plural pluperfect of dodi 'put' (-yssynt). nyt oed dim ohonaw 'there was nothing of him': ohonaw is o conjugated, third person masculine.

t: “Och!” heb vn o'r gwraged, “neur golles y mab.”
l: “Alas!” said one of the women, “has-been-lost the boy.”
i: “Alas!” said one of the women. “The boy is lost.”
n: Och is a cry of grief. vn 'one': the manuscript writes v for u here (vn = un); Evans prints it so, and it is kept. neur golles 'he has been lost': neur is the affirmative particle neu with the perfective particle ry, which softens colles to golles and gives the sense 'has'. colles is the third-person singular preterite of colli 'lose', here used without an object, 'be lost'.

t: “Ie,” heb arall, “bychan a dial oed yn lloski ni, neu yn dienydyaw am y mab.”
l: “Yes,” said another, “small vengeance it-was our burning us, or our executing for the boy.”
i: “Yes,” said another, “burning us or putting us to death would be small vengeance for the boy.”
n: oed 'was' stands for 'would be', as the imperfect often does in an unreal case. yn lloski ni 'our burning (us)': yn is the old spelling of ein 'our', the possessive serving as the object of the verbal noun (the Red Book writes an lloski). dienydyaw 'put to death'. bychan a dial 'small vengeance': the a between them is not clear (perhaps the linking particle); the Red Book has it too, and the sense is plain.

t: “A oes,” heb un o'r guraged, “kynghor o'r byt am hynn?”
l: “Is-there,” said one of the women, “a-counsel in the world about this?”
i: “Is there any counsel in the world,” said one of the women, “for this?”
n: A oes 'is there?': the question particle a with oes, the form of bot 'there is' used in questions and denials. guraged is gwraged spelt with gu (gw). kynghor o'r byt 'counsel of the world' = any counsel at all. hynn 'this'.

t: “Oes,” heb arall, “mi a wnn gynghor da,” heb hi.
l: “There-is,” said another, “I it-is-that know a-counsel good,” said she.
i: “There is,” said another. “I know a good counsel,” she said.
n: Oes 'there is' answers A oes by repeating the verb, the usual Welsh way of saying yes. mi a wnn 'I know': gwnn, the first-person singular present of gwybot, softened after a. gynghor ← kynghor, softened as the object after the verb and its subject.

t: “Beth yw hynny?” heb wy.
l: “What is that?” said they.
i: “What is that?” they said.
n: Beth 'what' is peth 'thing' softened, the usual form in questions. heb wy 'said they': wy is wynt 'they'.

t: “Gellast yssyd yma,” heb hi, “a chanawon genti.
l: “A-hound-bitch there-is here,” said she, “and whelps with-her.
i: “There is a hound bitch here,” she said, “with a litter of pups.
n: Gellast yssyd yma 'a hound bitch there is here': the indefinite subject first, then yssyd, the relative form of bot. gellast is a large hound bitch. a chanawon 'and whelps': kanawon (cenawon), spirant after a. genti 'with her' is gan conjugated, third person feminine.

t: Lladwn rei o'r canawon, ac irwn y hwyneb hitheu Riannon a'r gwaet, a'y dwylaw, a byrwn yr eskyrn gyr y bron, a thaerwn arnei e hun diuetha y mab.
l: Let-us-kill some of the whelps, and let-us-smear her face, hers, Rhiannon's, with the blood, and her hands, and let-us-throw the bones near her breast, and let-us-insist against-her herself destroying the boy.
i: Let us kill some of the pups and smear Rhiannon's face and hands with the blood, and throw the bones down beside her, and swear against her that she destroyed the boy herself.
n: Lladwn, irwn, byrwn, taerwn are first-person plural imperatives (-wn), 'let us kill, smear, throw, insist'. irwn is from iraw 'smear, anoint'; byrwn from bwrw 'throw'. y hwyneb 'her face': y 'her' puts h before a vowel. a'r gwaet 'with the blood' (a 'with'). a'y dwylaw 'and her hands' (dual of llaw). gyr y bron 'near her breast' (ger bron 'before, beside'). a thaerwn: taeru 'insist, maintain'. arnei 'against her' (ar, third person feminine). e hun 'herself'. diuetha 'destroying' (difetha), the verbal noun as the thing asserted.

t: Ac ni byd yn taered ni an chwech wrthi hi e hun.”
l: And there-will-not-be our insisting, us, our six, against her, herself.”
i: And her word alone will count for nothing against the six of us all insisting.”
n: The sentence is compressed and its exact construction is uncertain; the sense is that her denial alone will not stand against six of them. ni byd 'there will not be' (future of bot). yn taered ni 'our insistence': yn = ein 'our', taered 'obstinacy, insistence' (from taer). an chwech 'our six' = the six of us, an being another spelling of ein. wrthi hi e hun 'against her by herself': wrthi is wrth conjugated, third person feminine. The Red Book reads an taered ni an chwech.

t: Ac ar y kynghor hwnnw y trigwyt.
l: And on that counsel it-was-stayed.
i: And on that counsel they agreed.
n: y trigwyt 'it was stayed' is the impersonal preterite (-wyt) of trigaw 'stay, remain': they stayed with that counsel, they settled on it. The phrase ar y kynghor hwnnw is put first and the verb follows with y.

t: Parth a'r dyd Riannon a deffroes, ac a dywot, “A wraged,” heb hi, “mae y mab?”
l: Towards the day Rhiannon it-was-that woke, and that said, “O women,” said she, “where-is the boy?”
i: Towards daybreak Rhiannon woke, and said, “Women,” she said, “where is the boy?”
n: Riannon a deffroes 'Rhiannon woke', the abnormal sentence: deffroes is the third-person singular preterite of deffroi. ac a dywot 'and said': dywot is the third-person singular preterite of dywedut. A wraged 'O women': the vocative A softens gwraged. mae 'where is?' — the interrogative mae (modern ble mae).

t: “Arglwydes,” heb wy, “na ouyn di yni y mab.
l: “Lady,” said they, “do-not-ask you of-us the boy.
i: “Lady,” they said, “do not ask us for the boy.
n: Arglwydes 'lady', the title of a lord's wife. na ouyn di 'do not ask': gouyn 'ask', the second-person singular imperative, softened (g lost) after the negative na. yni 'of us' is y 'to' conjugated, first person plural (ynni below).

t: Nyt oes ohonam ni namyn cleisseu a dyrnodeu yn ymdaraw a thi; a diamheu yw gennym na welsam eiroet uilwraeth yn un wreic kymeint ac ynot ti.
l: There-is-not of-us but bruises and blows from struggling with you; and certain it-is with-us that we-never-saw ever warriorship in any woman as-much as in-you.
i: There is nothing left of us but bruises and blows from struggling with you; and we are certain we never saw such fighting spirit in any woman as in you.
n: Nyt oes ohonam ni namyn 'there is not of us but': ohonam is o conjugated, first person plural; namyn 'but, except'. cleisseu 'bruises' (cleis, modern clais); dyrnodeu 'blows' (dyrnawt). yn ymdaraw a thi 'struggling with you': ym- 'each other' + taraw 'strike'; a thi, ti with the spirant after a 'with'. diamheu 'without doubt'. na welsam 'that we did not see', first-person plural preterite of gwelet. uilwraeth ← milwraeth 'soldierly prowess', softened as object. yn un wreic 'in any woman' (gwreic softened after un). ynot 'in you' (yn, second person).

t: Ac ny thygyawd ynni ymdaraw a thi.
l: And it-did-not-avail to-us struggling with you.
i: And it was no use to us to struggle with you.
n: ny thygyawd 'it did not avail': tygyawd is the third-person singular preterite in -awd of tygyaw 'avail, succeed' (modern tycio), with the spirant after ny. ynni 'to us', y conjugated, first person plural.

t: Neur diffetheeist du hun dy uab, ac na hawl ef ynni.”
l: You-have-destroyed yourself your son, and do-not-claim him from-us.”
i: You have destroyed your own son, so do not demand him of us.”
n: Neur diffetheeist 'you have destroyed': neur is neu with the perfective ry, as before. diffetheeist is the second-person singular preterite of diffethaw (difetha; diuetha in the women's plot), written with a doubled e; both the White Book and the Red Book have the doubled form, and it is kept as written. du hun 'yourself' is dy hun with u for y (the Red Book has dy hun); kept as written. dy uab 'your son': mab softened after dy. na hawl 'do not claim', the second-person singular imperative of hawlyaw, after na.

t: “A druein,” heb y Riannon, “yr yr Arglwyd Duw a wyr pob peth, na yrrwch geu arnaf.
l: “Ah wretches,” said Rhiannon, “for the Lord God who knows every thing, do-not-drive a-lie upon-me.
i: “Ah, poor creatures,” said Rhiannon, “for the sake of the Lord God who knows all things, do not lay a lie upon me.
n: A druein 'O wretches': truein, plural of truan 'wretch', softened after the vocative A; the word pities as much as it rebukes. yr 'for the sake of' (er). a wyr 'who knows': gwyr, third-person singular present of gwybot, the g lost after a. na yrrwch 'do not drive': gyrru, second-person plural imperative, the g lost after na. geu 'lie, falsehood' (modern gau). arnaf 'on me' (ar, first person).

t: Duw, a wyr pob peth, a wyr bot yn eu hynny arnaf i.
l: God, who knows every thing, knows that being false that upon-me.
i: God, who knows all things, knows that it is false against me.
n: a wyr 'who knows' and a wyr 'knows' are the same verb twice: first the relative clause, then the main verb after its subject Duw. bot yn eu hynny 'that being false' = that that is false: eu is geu 'false' softened after the predicative yn: the soft mutation of g is its loss. arnaf i 'upon me', with the pronoun repeated.

t: Ac os ouyn yssyd arnawchi, ym kyffes y Duw, mi a'ch differaf.”
l: And if fear there-is on-you, by my confession to God, I it-is-that will-protect-you.”
i: And if you are afraid, by my confession to God, I will protect you.”
n: os 'if'. ouyn yssyd arnawchi 'fear there is on you' = you are afraid: arnawchi is arnawch chwi, ar conjugated, second person plural, with the pronoun written into it. ym kyffes y Duw 'by my confession to God': ym is a by-form of uy 'my'; the nasal mutation it should cause (kyffes > nghyffes) is not written. mi a'ch differaf 'I will protect you': 'ch the infixed 'you' (plural), differaf the first-person singular present of differaw 'protect, defend'.

t: “Dioer,” heb wy, “ny adwn ni drwc arnam ny hunein yr dyn yn y byt.”
l: “Assuredly,” said they, “we-will-not-let we evil upon-us ourselves for any-man in the world.”
i: “Indeed,” they said, “we will not bring harm on ourselves for anyone in the world.”
n: Dioer 'assuredly, indeed'. ny adwn 'we will not let': gadwn, first-person plural present of gadu 'let, leave', the g lost after ny. drwc ← drwg 'evil, harm', softened as the object after the verb and its subject. arnam 'on us'. ny hunein 'ourselves': ny is 'our' (ein) and hunein the plural of hun 'self'. yr dyn yn y byt 'for any man in the world' (yr 'for').

t: “A druein,” heb hitheu, “ny chewch un drwc yr dywedut y wirioned.”
l: “Ah wretches,” said she-for-her-part, “you-will-not-get any evil for telling the truth.”
i: “Ah, poor creatures,” she said, “you will come to no harm for telling the truth.”
n: heb hitheu 'said she for her part'. ny chewch 'you will not get': kewch, second-person plural present of caffael 'get', with the spirant after ny. un drwc 'any harm'. yr dywedut 'for telling': dywedut 'say, tell'. y wirioned 'the truth': gwirioned, feminine, softened after the article.

t: Yr a dywettei hi yn dec ac yn druan, ny chaffei namyn yr un atteb gan y gwraged.
l: For-all that she-would-say fairly and piteously, she-would-not-get but the one answer from the women.
i: For all she pleaded, fairly and piteously, she got no answer from the women but the same one.
n: Yr a dywettei hi 'for all that she would say': yr 'for' with the relative a; dywettei is the third-person singular imperfect of dywedut, with tt. yn dec 'fairly' ← teg and yn druan 'piteously' ← truan, adjectives made adverbs by yn, which softens them. ny chaffei 'she did not get': kaffei, third-person singular imperfect of caffael, with the spirant after ny. namyn yr un atteb 'but the one answer' = only the same answer.

t: Pwyll Penn Annwn ar hynny a gyuodes, a'r teulu a'r yniueroed, a chelu y damwein hwnnw ny allwyt.
l: Pwyll Head of-Annwfn at that it-was-that rose, and the household-troop and the hosts, and hiding that event could-not-be-done.
i: Pwyll, Head of Annwfn, rose at that, and his warband and companies, and there was no hiding what had happened.
n: Pwyll Penn Annwn … a gyuodes 'Pwyll Head of Annwfn rose': gyuodes ← kyuodes, third-person singular preterite of kyuodi, softened after a. Penn Annwn is the title he won in the first part; the spelling Annwn is the one this scribe uses here. teulu 'household troop', the lord's armed following; yniueroed 'hosts, companies' (niuer with a prefixed y). a chelu … ny allwyt 'and hiding … could not be done': kelu 'hide', spirant after a; allwyt is the impersonal preterite of gallu, the g lost after ny. damwein 'chance, event'.

t: Y'r wlat yd aeth y chwedyl, a phawb o'r guyrda a'e kigleu.
l: To the land it-was-that went the tale, and everyone of the noblemen heard-it.
i: The story went out into the land, and every one of the noblemen heard it.
n: Y'r wlat yd aeth 'into the land went': the phrase first, then yd (y before a vowel) and aeth, the third-person singular preterite of mynet. y chwedyl 'the tale, the news'. guyrda 'noblemen' (gwyrda; gu = gw). a'e kigleu 'heard it': relative a with the infixed 'e 'it'; kigleu is the old third-person singular preterite of klywet 'hear'.

t: A'r guyrda a doethant y gyt y wneuthur kynnadeu at Pwyll, y erchi idaw yscar a'e wreic, am gyflauan mor anwedus ac ar y wnaethoed.
l: And the noblemen it-was-that came together to make messengers to Pwyll, to ask of-him parting with his wife, for an-outrage as shameful as that she-had-done.
i: And the noblemen came together to send envoys to Pwyll, asking him to put away his wife for an outrage as shameful as the one she had done.
n: a doethant 'came' is plural, although a noun subject put first usually takes a singular verb; the plural here follows the sense. y wneuthur kynnadeu 'to make messengers' = to send envoys: gwneuthur softened after y 'to'; kynnadeu is the plural of kennat 'messenger'. y erchi idaw 'to ask of him'. yscar a 'part from' (ysgaru). gyflauan ← kyflauan 'outrage', softened after am. anwedus 'shameful'. ar y wnaethoed is best read as a ry wnaethoed, the relative a with the perfective particle ry, which softens gwnaethoed (third-person singular pluperfect of gwneuthur); the Red Book has ac a wnathoed.

t: Sef attep a rodes Pwyll, “Nyt oed achaws ganthunt wy y erchi y mi yscar a'm gwreic namyn na bydei plant idi.
l: That-is the answer that gave Pwyll: “There-was-not cause with-them, them, to ask of me parting with my wife but that there-would-not-be children to-her.
i: Pwyll answered: “They had no cause to ask me to put away my wife except that she had no children.
n: Sef attep a rodes Pwyll 'that is the answer Pwyll gave': rodes is the third-person singular preterite of rodi 'give'. attep 'answer' (ateb), -p for -b. ganthunt wy 'with them': gan conjugated, third person plural, with the pronoun repeated. a'm gwreic 'with my wife': a 'with' + 'm 'my'. namyn na bydei 'but that there would not be': bydei is the habitual imperfect of bot (modern byddai), 'that she would have no children' (the Red Book has namyn am na bydei). idi 'to her'.

t: Plant a wnn i y uot idi hi.
l: Children I it-is-that know their being to-her.
i: Children I know she has.
n: Plant a wnn i 'children I know': the object is put first, then a and the verb (gwnn, first person, softened). y uot idi hi 'its being to her' = that she has them: y 'its' softens bot to uot, and the singular y agrees with plant, which is a collective. idi hi 'to her', with the pronoun repeated. Pwyll means the son just born.

t: Ac nyt yscaraf a hi.
l: And I-will-not-part with her.
i: And I will not put her away.
n: nyt yscaraf 'I will not part': yscaraf is the first-person singular present, with future sense, of yscar. a hi 'with her'.

t: O gwnaeth hitheu gam, kymeret y phenyt amdanaw.”
l: If did she-for-her-part wrong, let-her-take her penance for-it.”
i: If she has done wrong, let her take her penance for it.”
n: O gwnaeth 'if she did': o 'if' (modern os) before a verb. hitheu 'she for her part'. gam ← cam 'wrong', softened as the object. kymeret is the third-person singular imperative of kymryt, 'let her take'. y phenyt 'her penance': penyt with the spirant after y 'her'. amdanaw 'for it' is am conjugated, third person masculine, pointing back to cam.

t: Hitheu Riannon a dyuynnwys attei athrawon a doethon.
l: She-for-her-part Rhiannon it-was-that summoned to-her teachers and wise-men.
i: Rhiannon, for her part, called teachers and wise men to her.
n: Hitheu Riannon 'she for her part, Rhiannon', the conjunctive pronoun with the name. a dyuynnwys 'summoned': the third-person singular preterite in -wys of dyuynnu (dyfynnu). attei 'to her' (at, third person feminine). athrawon, plural of athro 'teacher'; doethon 'wise men' (doeth 'wise').

t: A gwedy bot yn degach genthi kymryt y phenyt nog ymdaeru a'r gwraged, y phenyt a gymerth.
l: And after being fairer with-her to-take her penance than to-wrangle with the women, her penance she-took.
i: And since she thought it more seemly to take her penance than to dispute with the women, she took the penance.
n: gwedy bot 'after being' = since it was. yn degach 'fairer': tegach, comparative of teg, softened after the predicative yn. genthi 'with her' (gan, third person feminine): 'it seemed better to her'. nog is no 'than' before a vowel. ymdaeru 'dispute, wrangle' (ym- + taeru). y phenyt a gymerth 'her penance she took': object first; gymerth ← kymerth, third-person singular preterite of kymryt, softened after a.

t: Sef penyt a dodet erni, bot yn y llys honno yn Arberth hyt ym penn y seith mlyned.
l: That-is the penance that was-put on-her: being in that court in Arberth until the-end of the seven years.
i: The penance laid on her was to stay in that court at Arberth until the end of seven years.
n: Sef penyt a dodet erni 'that is the penance that was put on her': dodet is the impersonal preterite of dodi. erni is arni 'on her' spelt with e. bot 'being' gives the first term of the penance; the next unit continues it. y llys honno: llys is treated as feminine (honno). ym penn 'at the end' (yn + penn). seith mlyned 'seven years': blyned, the plural used after numbers, takes the nasal mutation after seith.

t: Ac yskynuaen a oed odieithyr y porth, eisted gyr llaw hwnnw beunyd, a dywedut y pawb a delei o'r a debygei nas gwyppei, y gyffranc oll, ac o'r a attei idi y dwyn, kynnic y westei a phellynic y dwyn ar y cheuyn y'r llys.
l: And a-mounting-block that-was outside the gate, sitting beside that daily, and telling to everyone that would-come, of-those that she-supposed that-he-would-not-know-it, the story all, and of-those that would-let to-her his carrying, offering to guest and to stranger his carrying on her back to the court.
i: There was a mounting-block outside the gate; she was to sit beside it every day and tell the whole story to everyone who came by whom she supposed not to know it, and to those who would let her carry them, to offer guest and stranger to carry them on her back to the court.
n: The penance continues in verbal nouns: eisted 'sitting', dywedut 'telling', kynnic 'offering'. yskynuaen 'mounting-block' (esgyn + maen). odieithyr 'outside'. gyr llaw 'beside'. beunyd 'daily'. delei is the third-person singular imperfect subjunctive of dyuot; debygei ← tybygei, imperfect of tybygu 'suppose'; nas gwyppei 'that he did not know it', 's 'it' with gwyppei, imperfect subjunctive of gwybot. y gyffranc 'the story': kyfranc, feminine, softened after the article. attei ← gattei, imperfect subjunctive of gadu 'let', the g lost after a. y westei ← gwestei 'guest', softened after y 'to'; a phellynic 'and stranger' (pellynic, modern pellennig). ar y cheuyn 'on her back': keuyn, spirant after y 'her'.

t: A damwein y gadei yr un y dwyn.
l: And by-chance it-was that would-let anyone his carrying.
i: And it was rare for anyone to let himself be carried.
n: damwein 'chance': 'it was a chance that' = only now and then. y gadei 'that would let': gadei, third-person singular imperfect of gadu 'let', used of what happened from time to time. yr un 'anyone'. y dwyn 'his carrying' = to be carried: y 'his' with the verbal noun.

t: Ac yuelly treulaw talym o'r ulwydyn a wnaeth.
l: And thus spending a-while of the year she-did.
i: And so she spent part of the year.
n: treulaw … a wnaeth 'spending she did' = she spent: the verbal-noun pattern. yuelly 'thus'. talym o'r ulwydyn 'a while of the year'.

t: Ac yn yr amser hwnnw yd oed yn arglwyd ar Wynt Ys Coet, Teirnon Twryf Uliant, a'r gwr goreu yn y byt oed.
l: And in that time there-was as lord over Gwent Is Coed, Teirnon Twrf Liant, and the best man in the world was-he.
i: At that time the lord of Gwent Is Coed was Teirnon Twrf Liant, and he was the best man in the world.
n: yd oed yn arglwyd 'there was as lord': yn makes arglwyd a predicate, and the subject, Teirnon, comes after. ar Wynt Ys Coet 'over Gwent Is Coed', the land of Gwent below the forest: Gwent, written Gwynt, softened after ar. Teirnon Twryf Uliant: the epithet is usually taken as twrf 'tumult, roar' + lliant 'flood, sea'; the manuscript writes it so here, and Toryfliant later. a'r gwr goreu yn y byt oed 'and the best man in the world he was': the predicate first, then the verb.

t: Ac yn y ty yd oed cassec.
l: And in the house there-was a-mare.
i: And in his house there was a mare.
n: yn y ty 'in the house': with 'his' one would expect the softened y dy, so y here is the article; i says 'his', since the house is Teirnon's. yd oed 'there was'. cassec 'mare' (caseg), -c for -g.

t: Ac nyt oed yn y dyrnas, na march na chassec degach no hi; a phob nos Calanmei y moei, ac ny wybydei neb un geir e wrth y hebawl.
l: And there-was-not in the kingdom, neither horse nor mare fairer than she; and every night of-the-Calends-of-May she-would-foal, and there-would-not-know anyone one word about her foal.
i: And in all the kingdom there was no horse or mare more beautiful than she; and every May Eve she would foal, and nobody knew a single word of what became of her foal.
n: y dyrnas 'the kingdom': tyrnas (teyrnas), feminine, softened after the article; the Red Book has teyrnas. na march na chassec 'neither horse nor mare' (kassec, spirant after na). degach ← tegach, softened after a feminine noun. nos Calanmei 'the night of the Calends of May', May Eve. y moei 'she would foal': moei is the imperfect of a verb moi used of a mare giving birth, the imperfect of something that happened again and again. ny wybydei 'did not know': gwybydei, imperfect of gwybot, softened after ny. geir 'word' (gair). e wrth 'about'. y hebawl 'her foal': ebawl with h after y 'her'.

t: Sef a wnaeth Teirnon, ymdidan nosweith a'y wreic, “Ha wreic,” heb ef; “llibin yd ym pob blwydyn yn gadu heppil yn cassec, heb gaffel yr un o honunt.”
l: That-is what did Teirnon: conversing one-night with his wife: “O wife,” said he, “feeble are-we every year in losing the offspring of our mare, without getting the one of-them.”
i: One night Teirnon talked with his wife. “Wife,” he said, “we are feckless, year after year losing our mare's foals without keeping a single one of them.”
n: Sef a wnaeth Teirnon, ymdidan 'that is what Teirnon did: conversing'. nosweith 'one night', an adverb of time. a'y wreic 'with his wife' (gwreic softened after 'y). Ha wreic 'O wife': Ha softens like A. llibin 'feeble, slack'. yd ym 'we are'. yn gadu heppil yn cassec 'leaving the offspring of our mare': gadu 'leave, lose'; yn is ein 'our', which puts h before a vowel (heppil ← eppil, modern epil). heb gaffel 'without getting' (kaffel, softened after heb). yr un o honunt 'a single one of them'.

t: “Peth a ellir wrth hynny?” heb hi.
l: “What can-be-done about that?” said she.
i: “What can be done about that?” she said.
n: Peth 'what', here unsoftened (beth elsewhere; the Red Book has Beth). a ellir 'that can be done': gellir is the impersonal present of gallu, the g lost after a. wrth hynny 'about that, against that'.

t: “Dial Duw arnaf,” heb ef, “nos Calanmei yw heno, ony wybydaf i pa dileith yssyd yn dwyn yr ebolyon.”
l: “The-vengeance of-God upon-me,” said he — “night of-the-Calends-of-May it-is tonight — unless I-find-out I what destruction that-is carrying the foals.”
i: “God's vengeance on me,” he said — “tonight is May Eve — if I do not find out what plague it is that carries off the foals.”
n: Dial Duw arnaf 'God's vengeance on me', an oath: may God punish me if I do not. The clause nos Calanmei yw heno 'May Eve it is tonight' stands between oath and condition. ony 'unless, if not'. wybydaf ← gwybydaf, first-person singular present (future) of gwybot, softened after ony. pa dileith 'what destruction': dileith (modern dilaith) 'ruin, destruction', a rare word. yssyd yn dwyn 'that is carrying off'. ebolyon, plural of ebawl.

t: Peri dwyn y gassec y mywn ty a wnaeth, a gwiscaw arueu amdanaw a oruc ynteu, a dechreu gwylat y nos.
l: Causing to-bring the mare into a-house he-did, and putting arms about-him he-did, he-for-his-part, and beginning to-watch the night.
i: He had the mare brought into a house, and he put on his arms and began to keep watch through the night.
n: Peri dwyn … a wnaeth 'causing to bring … he did' = he had (the mare) brought: peri 'cause' with a verbal noun. y gassec 'the mare': kassec, feminine, softened after the article. y mywn ty 'into a house'. gwiscaw arueu amdanaw a oruc ynteu 'putting arms about him he did': arueu (arfau) 'arms'; amdanaw 'about him' is am conjugated, third person masculine. a oruc and a wnaeth are the same 'he did'. dechreu gwylat 'beginning to watch' follows without a verb of its own.

t: Ac ual y byd dechreu noss, moi y gassec ar ebawl mawr telediw, ac yn seuyll yn y lle.
l: And as is the-beginning of night, foaling the mare of a foal big handsome, and standing on the spot.
i: And as night was coming on, the mare foaled a big, handsome foal, and it stood up at once.
n: ual y byd dechreu noss 'as is the beginning of night': byd, the consuetudinal present of bot, used here of a past moment. moi y gassec 'the mare foaling': the verbal noun moi with its subject after it carries the narrative. ar ebawl 'of a foal'. telediw 'handsome, well made'. ac yn seuyll yn y lle 'and standing on the spot': yn y lle 'at once'. ebawl is ebol (modern ebol), aw for o.

t: Sef a wnaeth Teirnon, kyuodi ac edrych ar prafter yr ebawl, ac ual y byd yuelly, ef a glywei twrwf mawr, ac yn ol y twrwf, llyma grauanc uawr drwy fenestyr ar y ty, ac yn ymauael a'r ebawl geir y uwng.
l: That-is what did Teirnon: rising and looking at the stoutness of the foal, and as he-is thus, he it-was-that heard a-noise great, and after the noise, behold a-claw great through a-window on the house, and grasping the foal by its mane.
i: Teirnon got up and looked at how sturdy the foal was; and as he stood so, he heard a great noise, and after the noise, there came a great claw through a window into the house and seized the foal by its mane.
n: kyuodi ac edrych 'rising and looking' answer Sef a wnaeth. prafter 'stoutness' (praff 'thick, stout'); after ar it should be softened (ar brafter), and is not. ual y byd yuelly 'as he is so', byd again of a past moment. ef a glywei 'he heard': glywei ← klywei, imperfect of klywet. twrwf 'tumult, noise' (twrf). llyma 'behold' throws the scene before your eyes. grauanc uawr: krauanc 'claw', softened after llyma, and mawr softened after the feminine noun. fenestyr 'window' is ffenestyr, f for ff. ymauael a 'take hold of'. geir y uwng 'by its mane': geir 'near, by' (ger), mwng softened after y 'its'.

t: Sef a wnaeth ynteu Teirnon, tynnu cledyf, a tharaw y ureich o not yr elin e ymdeith, ac yny uyd hynny o'r ureich a'r ebawl ganthaw ef y mywn.
l: That-is what did he-for-his-part Teirnon: drawing a-sword, and striking the arm from the-point of the elbow away, so-that is that of the arm and the foal with-him inside.
i: Teirnon drew his sword and struck off the arm at the elbow, so that that much of the arm, and the foal, were left inside with him.
n: tynnu cledyf 'drawing a sword'. a tharaw 'and striking' (taraw, spirant after a). y ureich 'the arm': breich, feminine, softened after the article. o not yr elin 'from the point of the elbow': not 'mark, point', elin 'elbow'. e ymdeith 'away' (ymaith). yny uyd 'so that there is': byd softened after yny 'until, so that', a present standing for the past. hynny o'r ureich 'that much of the arm'. ganthaw ef 'with him' (gan, third person masculine, with the pronoun). y mywn 'inside'.

t: Ac ar hynny twrwf, a diskyr a gigleu y gyt.
l: And at that a-noise and a-scream he-heard together.
i: And with that he heard a noise and a scream together.
n: Ac ar hynny 'and at that'. twrwf, a diskyr a gigleu 'a noise and a scream he heard': the objects first, then a and the verb. gigleu ← kigleu, the old third-person singular preterite of klywet, softened after a. diskyr 'scream, shriek' (disgyr). y gyt 'together'.

t: Agori y drws a oruc ef a dwyn ruthyr yn ol y twrwf.
l: Opening the door he-did, he, and bringing a-rush after the noise.
i: He opened the door and rushed out after the noise.
n: Agori … a oruc ef 'opening … he did' = he opened: agori is agor 'open'. a dwyn ruthyr 'and bringing a rush' = rushing: dwyn 'bring, carry', ruthyr (rhuthr) 'rush, onset'. yn ol 'after' (literally 'in the track of').

t: Ny welei ef y twrwf rac tywyllet y nos.
l: He-could-not-see he the noise for the-darkness of the night.
i: He could not see what made the noise, so dark was the night.
n: Ny welei ef 'he did not see': gwelei, third-person singular imperfect of gwelet, softened after ny. rac tywyllet y nos 'because of how dark the night was': rac 'for, because of' with tywyllet, the equative of tywyll 'dark', used as a noun of degree.

t: Ruthyr a duc yn y ol, a'y ymlit.
l: A-rush he-brought after it, and its pursuing.
i: He rushed after it and chased it.
n: Ruthyr a duc 'a rush he brought' = he rushed: object first, then a and duc, the third-person singular preterite of dwyn. yn y ol 'after it' (in its track). a'y ymlit 'and its pursuing' = and pursued it: 'y 'its' as the object of the verbal noun ymlit 'pursue'.

t: A dyuot cof idaw adaw y drws yn agoret, ac ymhwelut a wnaeth.
l: And coming memory to-him of-leaving the door open, and turning-back he-did.
i: Then he remembered that he had left the door open, and he turned back.
n: A dyuot cof idaw 'and memory coming to him' = he remembered. adaw 'leaving' (gadael). yn agoret 'open': Evans prints the n of yn as a raised letter, which the second witness drops (y agoret); the reading yn agoret is certain on the image. agoret is the participle of agori. ymhwelut 'turn back' is ymchwelut written with hw for chw (the Red Book has ymchoelut). a wnaeth closes the verbal-noun narrative.

t: Ac wrth y drws, llyma uab bychan yn y gorn, guedy troi llenn o bali yn y gylch.
l: And by the door, behold a-boy little in his swaddling(?), after wrapping a-mantle of brocade around-him.
i: And there by the door lay a little boy in swaddling clothes, with a mantle of brocade wrapped around him.
n: llyma uab bychan 'behold a little boy': mab softened after llyma. yn y gorn: gorn is the softened form after y 'his' of corn, apparently here a wrapping or swaddling for an infant; the sense is uncertain, and i takes it as swaddling clothes. guedy troi 'after wrapping', gwedy with a verbal noun = having been wrapped. llenn 'mantle, sheet' (llen). o bali 'of brocade': pali softened after o. yn y gylch 'around him': kylch softened after y 'his'.

t: Kymryt y mab a wnaeth attaw, a llyma y mab yn gryf yn yr oet a oed arnaw.
l: Taking the boy he-did to-him, and behold the boy strong in the age that was on-him.
i: He took the boy up to him, and the boy was strong for the age he was.
n: Kymryt … a wnaeth attaw 'taking … he did to him' = he took him up: attaw is at conjugated, third person masculine. llyma y mab yn gryf 'behold the boy strong': kryf softened after the predicative yn. yn yr oet a oed arnaw 'in the age that was on him' = for his age: oet here 'age' (the same word as oet 'appointment').

t: Dodi cayat ar y drws a wnaeth, a chyrchu yr ystauell yd oed y wreic yndi.
l: Putting a-closing on the door he-did, and making-for the chamber that was the wife in-it.
i: He shut the door and went to the chamber where his wife was.
n: Dodi cayat ar y drws 'putting a closing on the door' = shutting it: cayat 'closing, shutting' (from cau). a chyrchu 'and making for' (kyrchu, spirant after a). yr ystauell yd oed y wreic yndi 'the chamber that the wife was in it': Welsh puts the preposition at the end with a pronoun, yndi 'in it' (yn, third person feminine, for the feminine ystauell). y wreic: gwreic softened after the article; 'his wife' in i.

t: “Arglwydes,” heb ef, “ay kyscu yd wyt ti?”
l: “Lady,” said he, “is-it sleeping that you-are you?”
i: “Lady,” he said, “are you asleep?”
n: ay kyscu yd wyt ti 'is it sleeping that you are?': ay (modern ai) asks about a word put first, here the verbal noun kyscu, which it does not soften. yd wyt 'you are', with yd before the vowel.

t: “Nac ef, Arglwyd,” heb hi.
l: “Not so, Lord,” said she.
i: “No, Lord,” she said.
n: Nac ef 'not it' = no: the negative of answers (nac before a vowel) with ef 'it'. Arglwyd 'Lord', her address to her husband.

t: “Mi a gyskeis, a phan doethost ti y mywn mi a deffroeis.”
l: “I it-is-that slept, and when you-came you in I it-is-that woke.”
i: “I was asleep, and when you came in I woke.”
n: mi a gyskeis 'I slept': kyskeis, first-person singular preterite of kyscu, softened after a. a phan 'and when'. doethost 'you came', second-person singular preterite of dyuot. y mywn 'in'. deffroeis 'I woke', first-person singular preterite. Both sentences are the abnormal order with mi.

t: “Mae ymma mab it,” heb ef, “os mynny, yr hwnn ny bu yt eiroet.”
l: “There-is here a-son for-you,” said he, “if you-wish, the one that there-was-not to-you ever.”
i: “Here is a son for you,” he said, “if you want him, the son you never had.”
n: Mae ymma 'there is here'. it 'for you' and yt are two spellings of y 'to' conjugated, second person singular. os mynny 'if you wish': mynny, second-person singular present of mynnu. yr hwnn 'the one that'. ny bu 'there was not': bu, third-person singular preterite of bot. eiroet 'ever' (erioed).

t: “Arglwyd,” heb hi, “pa gyfranc uu hynny?”
l: “Lord,” said she, “what adventure was that?”
i: “Lord,” she said, “what happened?”
n: pa gyfranc 'what adventure': kyfranc 'encounter, adventure, story', softened after pa. uu ← bu, preterite of bot, softened as after a relative a, which is often left unwritten before forms of bot.

t: “Llyma oll,” heb y Teirnon, a menegi y dadyl oll.
l: “Behold all,” said Teirnon, and telling the account all.
i: “Here is the whole of it,” said Teirnon, and he told her the whole story.
n: Llyma oll 'here is all' = here is the whole of it. a menegi 'and telling': the verbal noun carries on after the speech, as if a wnaeth followed; menegi is mynegi 'tell, declare'. y dadyl 'the account': dadyl (dadl), d = dd.

t: “Ie, Arglwyd,” heb hi, “pa ryw wisc yssyd am y mab?”
l: “Yes, Lord,” said she, “what kind-of garment is-there about the boy?”
i: “Yes, Lord,” she said, “and what sort of garment is the boy wrapped in?”
n: pa ryw wisc 'what kind of garment': ryw ← rhyw softened after pa, and gwisc softened after ryw. yssyd 'that is'. am y mab 'about the boy': clothing is 'about' a person.

t: “Llen o bali,” heb ynteu.
l: “A-mantle of brocade,” said he-for-his-part.
i: “A mantle of brocade,” he said.
n: Llen 'mantle', here with one n (llenn above). o bali 'of brocade' (pali softened after o). heb ynteu 'said he for his part'.

t: “Mab y dynnyon mwyn yw,” heb hi.
l: “A-son to people gentle he-is,” said she.
i: “He is a son of gentle birth,” she said.
n: Mab … yw 'a son … he is': the predicate first, then yw. y dynnyon mwyn 'to gentle people': dynnyon is dynion 'people' (the softening after y 'to' does not show, d being written for dd); mwyn 'gentle, well-born'. Pali, silk brocade, was a rich man's cloth, and she reads the boy's birth from it.

t: “Arglwyd,” heb hi, “digrifwch a didanwch oed gennyf i, bei mynnut ti, mi a dygwn wraged yn un a mi, ac a dywedwn uy mot y ueichawc.”
l: “Lord,” said she, “amusement and comfort it-was with-me, if you-wished you, I it-is-that would-bring women at one with me, and that would-say my being pregnant.”
i: “Lord,” she said, “it would be a pleasure and a comfort to me, if you would agree, for me to bring some women into my confidence and say that I had been with child.”
n: digrifwch 'amusement, pleasure'; didanwch 'comfort, consolation'. oed 'was' for 'would be'. bei mynnut ti 'if you would wish': bei 'if', mynnut the second-person singular imperfect subjunctive of mynnu. mi a dygwn 'I would bring', first-person singular imperfect of dwyn, softened after a; a dywedwn 'and would say', of dywedut. yn un a mi 'at one with me', in league with me. uy mot 'my being': bot with the nasal mutation after uy 'my'. y ueichawc 'pregnant': beichawc softened as after the predicative yn; the Red Book has yn ueichawc.

t: “Myui a duunaf a thi yn llawen,” heb ef, “am hynny.”
l: “I-myself will-agree with you gladly,” said he, “about that.”
i: “I will gladly agree with you,” he said, “in that.”
n: Myui 'I myself' (myfi), the emphatic pronoun, put first: Myui a duunaf 'I will agree'. duunaf is the first-person singular present, with future sense, of duunaw 'agree, be of one mind' (dy- + un 'one'). a thi 'with you' (spirant after a). yn llawen 'gladly'.

t: Ac yuelly y gwnaethpwyt.
l: And thus it-was-done.
i: And so it was done.
n: y gwnaethpwyt 'it was done': the impersonal preterite of gwneuthur, unsoftened after the particle y.

t: Peri a wnaethont bedydyaw y mab, o'r bedyd a wneit yna.
l: Causing they-did to-baptize the boy, of the baptism that was-done then.
i: They had the boy baptized, with the baptism that was used at that time.
n: Peri a wnaethont bedydyaw 'causing they did to baptize' = they had (him) baptized. bedydyaw (bedyddio), from bedyd 'baptism', with d = dd. o'r bedyd a wneit yna 'of the baptism that was done then': wneit ← gwneit, the impersonal imperfect of gwneuthur, softened after a; the storyteller marks the baptism as the custom of that time.

t: Sef enw a dodet arnaw, Gwri Wallt Euryn.
l: That-is the name that was-put on-him: Gwri Wallt Euryn.
i: The name they gave him was Gwri Wallt Euryn.
n: Sef enw a dodet arnaw 'that is the name that was put on him': dodet, impersonal preterite of dodi; arnaw 'on him' (ar, third person masculine). Gwri Wallt Euryn 'Gwri of the golden hair': gwallt 'hair' softened in an epithet after the name, and euryn 'golden' (from eur 'gold'). The next unit explains the name.

t: Yr hynn a oed ar y ben o wallt, kyuelynet oed a'r eur.
l: What was on his head of hair, as-yellow was-it as the gold.
i: What hair he had on his head was as yellow as gold.
n: Yr hynn a oed ar y ben o wallt 'that which was on his head of hair' = the hair on his head: y ben ← pen, softened after y 'his'; o wallt ← gwallt, softened after o. kyuelynet oed a'r eur 'as yellow it was as the gold': kyuelynet is the equative of melyn 'yellow' (modern cyfelyn), and a 'as' completes it.
